Project construction may start immediately and must be completed by October 4, 2023. Due to the year around spawning period for surf smelt in this portion of Puget Sound and other fish and shellfish habitats present at the job site, work will be allowed from September 1 through December 31 and January 1 through March 1 of any year if a biologist approved by the Department of Fish and Wildlife does not detect surf smelt eggs during a beach survey. Work must begin within seventy-two hours of survey and you must complete the work within two weeks of the survey. The biologist must follow the department-approved intertidal forage fish spawning protocol and use the standard department data sheets when conducting forage fish spawning beach surveys. A list of certified biologists, the approved protocol and data sheets are available on the department's web site http://wdfw.wa.gov/licensing/hpa/technical_assistance.html . The biologist must submit the completed, data sheets to the department within seventy-two hours of completing the survey to WDFW by e-mail at HPAapplications@dfw.wa.gov; mail to Post Office Box 43234, Olympia, Washington 98504-3234; or fax to (360) 902- 2946. In addition, the biologist must preserve the winnowed portion of the sediment samples and retain them for a minimum of four weeks. The sediment samples must be provided to WDFW staff upon request.

summary.text: The Port of Friday Harbor (Port) proposes to remove overwater piers and pilings associated with the Jackson Beach Cannery Facility (Facility). The purpose of this project is to restore ecological function of the shoreline, intertidal, and subtidal environment through the removal of creosote-treated timber over- and in-water structures. The Facility structures served pervious industrial uses that are no longer active. Creosote is known to be toxic, carcinogenic, and persistent deleterious substance present in marine environments, which results in adverse effects to fish, invertebrates, and other aquatic organisms. Removal of these structures will eliminate a source of chemical contamination to the marine ecosystem surrounding the Facility. Additionally,removal of overwater structures from shoreline, intertidal, and shallow subtidal areas will improve habitat critical for sensitive species. The existing structures degrade critical shoreline, intertidal, and shallow subtidal habitat, limiting the growth of marine vegetation, such as eelgrass (Zostera marina) and reducing the ecological productivity of these sensitive areas. Shoreline habitat is used by juvenile salmonids for foraging and rearing. Removal of these structures reestablishes natural light penetration, improves sediment conditions, and supports the long-term recovery of native shoreline and nearshore habitats.

The proposed action is necessary to effectively remove chemical contamination, particularly TBT, in a shallow subtidal region that was impacted from boat maintenance and repair activities associated with the tidal grid and wood plank pier that were conducted prior to 1986. The remediation area is approximately 40 feet by 60 feet and extends north and south of both finger piers and underneath the main concrete pier. Sediment would be dredged using a diver-assisted hydraulic dredge. Based on results from previous sediment investigations, four feet of sediment would be removed from the remediation area. Dredged sediment would be pumped to a nearby barge fitted with Geotubes used to de-water the dredged sediment. The Geotubes would be inoculated with project-specific polymers to bind with suspended solids in the dredged material slurry, resulting in a clear effluent. Resulting water would be contained within the barge until it can be tested to ensure it meets standards established by the Department of Ecology. Once the effluent meets applicable standards, it would be discharged back into West Sound. Once dewatering is completed, the barge would be towed to the Waste Management transload facility on the Duwamish Waterway in Seattle. trail.title: Ecology PARIS: Numeric effluent violation; Effluent Violations; DMR note = "TSS percent removal was below 85% due to chlorinating return activated sludge to control filaments." Jankowiak - calculation correct. dilute influent also. TSS effluent up to mid 20's. Discuss chlorination technique and other options for filament control. Laz - Plant had a couple of high effluent solids for the month.  The first part of the month operator had to chlorinate the RAS to reduce filaments and consequently the effluent TSS got worse. Coupled with the high rainfall and snow melt events operator was unable to meet the percent removal requirements. Operator's calculations show that plant would have to be below 5.25 mg/l TSS to make 85%. According to Mr. Light, "that is asking a lot if the plant is not running perfectly". Roy Light contacted Carl for assistance, and discussed adding chlorine, but that at a certain point, will make turbid. Looks like effluent/filament control improving. Other methods for control, not really ideal there. Discussion of other methods, preventing filamentous in the first place and how apply chlorine (ideally directly to RAS). Decision - Carl to follow-up.  Warning letter for violation.

Ecology PARIS: Numeric effluent violation; Effluent Violations; Jankowiak: calculation correct. Inf TSS very low (15-27 mg/l) - check if correct.  No DMR note on violation. Contact Eastsound to verify. Eleuterio: Mr. Roy Light is not positive of the cause. He suspects that the person doing the laboratory analysis was not mixing the samples thoroughly. Mr. Light observed the lab technician doing the testing and found that he was not shaking the sample enough.  It also affected the Orcas Village influent samples and the cellulose standard. The problem has been corrected.

aq-143315.title: Ecology federal permits record: Lawson Pond Dam Replacement (Aquatics 143315)

rows.label: What the project is
rows.value: The project proposes to remove an existing earthen dam and 18-inch culvert spillway to install a replacement dam and replacement outfall spillway within Lawson Pond on San Juan Island. The Washington State Dam Safety Office (DSO) has determined that the current dam, created in the 1940s, no longer meets modern safety requirements and needs to be replaced. The dam and outfall replacement structures would occur within the same footprint as the existing structures. The outfall spillway of Lawson Pond would be replaced with two 24-inch culverts and a narrow emergency spillway located above the replacement culverts. At least 20 linear feet of the outflow stream channel would be armored with quarry spall rock as an erosion control measure as required by DSO. The armored channel would then be hydroseeded with a riparian/wetland herbaceous seed mix for partial herbaceous cover sprouting between the rocks. During construction, the pond would be temporarily dewatered. The underwater topography slopes uniformly to the dam, and extensive bedrock makes the installation of a cofferdam impractical. Dewatering will also eradicate largemouth bass, which are the only fish present in the Pond according to a 2024 fish survey by West Fork Environmental. Pumps, existing water pipes and temporary hoses would be used to gradually dewater Lawson Pond, and water would be discharged onto the uplands of adjacent farm pastures utilizing an existing water right. The secondary dewatering option in case discharge to adjacent farm pastures is not enough is pumping into upland forests east of Lawson Pond

rows.label: What the project is
rows.value: The Port of Friday Harbor (Port) proposes to remove overwater piers and pilings associated with the Jackson Beach Cannery Facility (Facility). The purpose of this project is to restore ecological function of the shoreline, intertidal, and subtidal environment through the removal of creosote-treated timber over- and in-water structures. The Facility structures served pervious industrial uses that are no longer active. Creosote is known to be toxic, carcinogenic, and persistent deleterious substance present in marine environments, which results in adverse effects to fish, invertebrates, and other aquatic organisms. Removal of these structures will eliminate a source of chemical contamination to the marine ecosystem surrounding the Facility. Additionally,removal of overwater structures from shoreline, intertidal, and shallow subtidal areas will improve habitat critical for sensitive species. The existing structures degrade critical shoreline, intertidal, and shallow subtidal habitat, limiting the growth of marine vegetation, such as eelgrass (Zostera marina) and reducing the ecological productivity of these sensitive areas. Shoreline habitat is used by juvenile salmonids for foraging and rearing. Removal of these structures reestablishes natural light penetration, improves sediment conditions, and supports the long-term recovery of native shoreline and nearshore habitats.

rows.label: What the project is
rows.value: Dredge up to 360 cubic yards of sediment in a shallow subtidal region next to an existing concrete pier within West Sound on Orcas Island, San Juan County, Washington. The proposed action is necessary to effectively remove chemical contamination, particularly TBT, in a shallow subtidal region that was impacted from boat maintenance and repair activities associated with the tidal grid and wood plank pier that were conducted prior to 1986. The remediation area is approximately 40 feet by 60 feet and extends north and south of both finger piers and underneath the main concrete pier. Sediment would be dredged using a diver-assisted hydraulic dredge. Based on results from previous sediment investigations, four feet of sediment would be removed from the remediation area. Dredged sediment would be pumped to a nearby barge fitted with Geotubes used to de-water the dredged sediment. The Geotubes would be inoculated with project-specific polymers to bind with suspended solids in the dredged material slurry, resulting in a clear effluent. Resulting water would be contained within the barge until it can be tested to ensure it meets standards established by the Department of Ecology. Once the effluent meets applicable standards, it would be discharged back into West Sound. Once dewatering is completed, the barge would be towed to the Waste Management transload facility on the Duwamish Waterway in Seattle. The Geotubes would be removed from the barge and loaded on either a truck or train for transport to a Subtitle D landfill.
